1	# Depth Over Breadth: Designing Modules for the Next Reader
2
3	By Priya Okafor · https://example.com/essays/depth-over-breadth
4
5	Most advice about modules is about size. This essay argues that size is the wrong axis. What matters is how much a module asks of the people who call it, compared with how much it does for them.
6
7	## Deep modules
8
9	A deep module does a lot of work behind a small interface. The caller learns a handful of things and gets a great deal of behaviour in return. A file system is the classic example: open, read, write, close, and behind those four calls sit caching, scheduling, permissions, and recovery from crashes. Depth is a ratio, so a module can only be judged deep or shallow once you know what its interface is.
10
11	## Shallow modules
12
13	A shallow module is the opposite: its interface is nearly as complicated as what it does. A class that wraps one database call behind a constructor, three setters, and an `execute` method makes every caller learn five things to save one line. Splitting code into many shallow modules adds interfaces without adding depth, and the total that readers must learn goes up.
14
15	## Interface
16
17	By interface I do not mean a language keyword. A module's interface is everything a caller must know to use it correctly: the names and types of its operations, and also what each operation assumes, what it guarantees, what errors it raises, what order calls must come in, and how fast it is. Much of the interface is never written in code, which is why it is easy to underestimate.
18
19	## Signature
20
21	A signature is the part of the interface a compiler can check: an operation's name, its parameter types, and its return type. Two functions can share a signature and have very different interfaces, because the signature says nothing about side effects, ordering, or what happens on failure. Treating the signature as the whole interface is the most common way designers fool themselves into thinking a module is simple.
22
23	## API
24
25	An API is an interface offered across a boundary to code you do not control, such as another team, another service, or the public. Every API is an interface, but not every interface is an API: the interface between two classes in the same package is not one. The distinction matters because an API is expensive to change. Once outside code depends on it, every part of its interface, including the unwritten parts, becomes a promise.
26
27	## Information hiding
28
29	Deep modules are built by information hiding: deciding which design decisions live inside the module and keeping them out of the interface. Every decision that leaks into the interface becomes something callers depend on and something you can no longer change freely.
30
31	## Leaky abstractions
32
33	An abstraction leaks when callers must know about a hidden detail to use the module correctly, such as a remote call that is slow or fails in ways a local call never would. A leak quietly widens the interface: the detail was supposed to be hidden, but now every caller has to know it. Most leaks are not bugs in the code. They are parts of the interface the designer never admitted were there.
34

5	# Information Hiding
6
7	Information hiding is the practice of keeping a module's design decisions, such as its data layout or algorithm, inside the module, so callers cannot come to depend on them and the decisions can change without breaking anyone.
8
9	It is like a restaurant kitchen behind a pass: diners order from the menu and never see, or rely on, how the cooks organise the line.
10
11	A date library stores timestamps as nanoseconds internally but exposes only `before`, `after`, and `format`, so switching to microseconds later breaks no caller.

6
7	An idempotency key is a unique value a client attaches to a request so the server can recognise a repeat of that request and return the first result instead of performing the work again.

# Deep Module

A deep module does a lot of work behind a small interface, so callers learn a few things and get a great deal of behaviour in return. Depth is a ratio of what the module does to what its interface asks of callers, so you can only call a module deep once you know its whole interface, not just its signatures.

It is like a light switch: one control, and behind it sit the wiring, the breakers, and the power grid, none of which you have to think about.

Unix file I/O is the classic case. Callers learn `open`, `read`, `write`, and `close`. Behind those four calls sit caching, disk scheduling, permissions, and crash recovery.

# Signature

A signature is the part of an interface a compiler can check: an operation's name, its parameter types, and its return type. It says nothing about side effects, call order, or what happens on failure, so two functions with the same signature can have very different interfaces.

It is like the label on a jar: it gives the name and the weight, but not whether the contents have gone off or need to be refrigerated once opened.

`save(user: User): void` could write to an in-memory map, or it could call a remote database that can time out and only works after `connect()`. The signature is the same, but the interfaces are very different.

# Leaky Abstraction

An abstraction leaks when callers have to know about a detail it was meant to hide in order to use it correctly. A leak quietly widens the interface, because now every caller has to learn that detail. Most leaks are not bugs. They are parts of the interface the designer never admitted were there.

It is like a rental car that pulls to the left: you were told you only need to steer, but now every driver has to know about the wheel alignment.

An ORM makes `user.orders` look like a field read, but each access runs a database query. Loop over 1,000 users and you make 1,000 queries, so callers need to know about the database after all.

Links: [[Information Hiding]], [[Interface]], [[Deep Module]], [[Software Design]], [[Depth Over Breadth]]

# Interface

A module's interface is everything a caller must know to use it correctly. That includes the names and types of its operations, and also what each one assumes, what it guarantees, which errors it raises, what order calls must come in, and how fast it is. Much of an interface is never written in code, which makes it easy to underestimate. This is broader than the `interface` keyword in Java or TypeScript, which only declares [[Signature|signatures]].

It is like a full job description, not just the list of duties: it also covers the hours, who you report to, and what gets you fired. A candidate who reads only the duties will get surprised.

`withdraw(amount)` takes a number and returns nothing. Its interface also says the amount must be positive, that it throws `InsufficientFunds`, that `open()` must be called first, and that it makes a network call that can take seconds.

# API

An API is an interface offered across a boundary to code you don't control, such as another team, another service, or the public. Every API is an interface, but an interface between two classes in the same package is not an API. APIs are expensive to change: once outside code depends on one, every part of its interface becomes a promise, including the parts that were never written down.

It is like a published train timetable compared with the crew's internal rota. The crew can reshuffle the rota freely, but once passengers plan around the timetable, any change breaks their plans.

A payments service happens to return transactions sorted by date, though its docs never say so. Partner code starts relying on that order, so changing the sort becomes a breaking change.
